notes: "The two friends were big now." reads a little childish; "The two friends were grown up now." is more natural and still A1.
"Kai tied his little sled to hers." works, though Kai's sled is introduced only by the possessive; optional: "Kai had a little sled. He tied it to hers."

"Before she left, the queen gave him a task." comes after the description of Kai working, so the order is slightly backwards. Acceptable at A2 without the past perfect; optional: move it before "He moved flat pieces of ice...".
"his tears washed the splinter out": two splinters were introduced earlier. Optional clarity: "washed the splinter out of his eye".
'forever' stands in for Andersen's 'Eternity'. That is a fine simplification and matches A1/B1.

"'She was going to Lapland,' said an old reindeer": in Andersen the pigeons guess Lapland and the reindeer only says Lapland is his home. The line is harmless, but more faithful: "'Lapland is my home,' said an old reindeer that stood near them."
"Gerda had no boots and no gloves": gloves/mittens were never given to her at this level. Optional: "Gerda had no boots".
"The troll's students": "pupils" or "helpers" fits a fairy tale better (taste).

"how far she has walked on her bare feet" is faithful to Andersen, but B2 never says outright that Gerda was barefoot (it is only implied when she offers her shoes to the river), and she wears the prince's boots by then. Optional: add "barefoot" to "She ran out of the garden", as C1 does.
"In fact two splinters of the troll's mirror were inside him." "In fact" is slightly flat; "In truth" or simply "Two splinters..." reads better (taste).
"snowflakes under a glass": Andersen's is a magnifying glass. "under a magnifying glass" avoids reading it as a glass dome.

"The reindeer carried them home past the women of Finland and Lapland" followed by "Spring came with them as they walked" sits slightly uneasily. Andersen's reindeer takes them only to the border. Optional: "carried them south ... to the edge of the snow".
The literary register is genuine and well sustained: squeaking boots, the newspapers, porcupine snowflakes, skates, the volcanoes and the robber girl's barb are all authentic Andersen details.

summary: All five levels follow Andersen's seven-story arc in order, from the troll's mirror to the grown-up children in summer, with no film-derived elements. Grammar matches each level and the quizzes have single, correctly keyed answers. Remaining points are minor clarity and taste notes, chiefly the unestablished 'bare feet' line in B2 and the reindeer/walking overlap in C1's ending.
